title: SME Self-Quiz
description: The self-quiz questions from the SME Prep hub (Weeks 1–5), tagged by chapter.

questions.prompt: During a staff meeting, a marketing director spends 20 minutes telling her team what she learned at last week’s industry conference. Which Mintzberg role is she performing?
questions.explanation: She is sending information to people inside the organization. Spokesperson sends it outside. Monitor was the act of gathering it at the conference, which already happened. Liaison is about keeping horizontal contacts.

questions.prompt: A manager flies to a trade show mainly to learn what competitors are launching next year. Which role?
questions.explanation: Monitor: scanning the environment for information and trends. Disseminating would be sharing it internally afterwards.

questions.prompt: A CEO gives a televised interview explaining the firm’s quarterly results. Which role?
questions.explanation: Spokesperson sends information into the external environment (media, shareholders). Figurehead is symbolic duty, not information transmission.

questions.prompt: A supervisor steps in to stop a shouting match between two reps and then decides who gets first pick of overtime. Which two decisional roles?
questions.explanation: Handling conflict = disturbance handler. Deploying a scarce resource (overtime) = resource allocator. Both are decisional roles.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Weber’s qualities of bureaucracy?

options.text: Decentralized decision making by front-line employees
Selection and promotion based on technical skill

questions.explanation: Weber called for centralization of power at the top. Decentralization is the opposite, and it’s what the human relations critics wanted.

questions.prompt: The Hawthorne studies are most closely associated with the rise of:
questions.explanation: Hawthorne showed that social and psychological factors affect productivity, and that launched the human relations movement.

questions.prompt: A manager can reliably tell when two senior developers will threaten to quit after a product launch, but has no idea why. This illustrates which goal of OB?
questions.explanation: Anticipating behaviour without knowing the cause is predicting. "Contingency planning" isn’t one of the three goals.

questions.prompt: A firm manages its payroll unit with tight procedures and its R&D unit with loose, flexible rules. This best reflects:
questions.explanation: Matching the style to the demands of each unit’s situation is the contingency approach, and this is the textbook’s own example.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of Kotter’s three elements of what effective general managers do?
questions.explanation: Functional foremanship is Taylor’s idea (supervisors specialize by function).

questions.prompt: According to Luthans and colleagues, managers who spend the most time networking tend to:

options.text: Be promoted fastest, though their units aren’t the most effective

questions.explanation: Networking brings the fastest promotion. Time on HRM brings the most effective units and the most satisfied employees. It’s a trade-off.

questions.prompt: Psychological capital (PsyCap) falls under which contemporary management concern?
questions.explanation: PsyCap (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) is the basis of positive OB, which sits under employee health and well-being.

questions.prompt: Work that is risky, uncertain and unpredictable, with low or unreliable pay and few protections, is called:
questions.explanation: Precarious work, which falls under alternative work arrangements.

questions.prompt: Work engagement is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Engagement = vigour, dedication, absorption. Hope/efficacy/resilience/optimism is PsyCap. Meaning/purpose/community is spirituality. Vitality + learning is thriving.

questions.prompt: Which is part of the human relations critique of bureaucracy?

options.text: Impersonal rules become a performance ceiling: the minimum becomes the norm
Promotion on technical skill encourages nepotism
Specialization increases commitment to overall goals

questions.explanation: Rules set a minimum acceptable level that turns into the ceiling. The other options reverse the critique: centralization wastes ideas, and specialization causes the red-tape mentality.

questions.prompt: Taylor’s scientific management focused mainly on:

options.text: Designing and standardizing individual jobs on the shop floor
Organization-wide chain of command and promotion rules

questions.explanation: Taylor = job design and standardizing physical work. Chain of command and promotion rules are Weber’s bureaucracy.

questions.prompt: In the handout’s S + T = R, the "T" stands for:

options.text: Thinking: the person’s interpretation of the situation

questions.explanation: Situation + Thinking = Response. People respond to how they interpret a situation, not to the situation itself.

questions.prompt: In the thermostat analogy, what comes first, and with what tool?

options.text: Assess the current state with a SWOT analysis
Set the desired state with a mission statement
Close the gap with an action plan
Measure results with a balanced scorecard

questions.explanation: Read, Set, Close, Check: step 1 is the current state, diagnosed with SWOT.

questions.prompt: A firm donates to local shelters and cuts packaging waste. It also runs pay-equity reviews for its own staff. The pay-equity reviews are an example of:
questions.explanation: CSR aimed at the workforce is internal CSR. The community and environment work is external CSR.

questions.prompt: Which Big Five dimension predicts job performance most consistently across virtually all occupations?
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness is the strongest, most universal predictor. Extraversion matters mostly in interpersonal jobs, openness in creative ones, and agreeableness in helping and teamwork jobs.

questions.prompt: Deja believes her promotions depend on connections and luck, so she rarely bothers with extra training. She is displaying:
questions.explanation: Beliefs that outside forces control outcomes = external locus of control. CSE is a four-trait bundle, and the scenario gives no evidence on the other three.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the four core self-evaluation traits?
questions.explanation: CSE = self-esteem, general self-efficacy, locus of control and neuroticism. Extraversion is the classic distractor.

questions.prompt: According to the textbook, positive and negative affectivity are:
questions.explanation: PA and NA are independent, not opposites. This is a common true/false trap.

questions.prompt: Personality traits are most likely to influence behaviour in:

options.text: Weak situations with loosely defined roles and few rules
Strong situations with clear rules and rewards

questions.explanation: Weak situations let personality show. Strong situations constrain it (interactionist view).

questions.prompt: An employee got the raise she felt she deserved, but her manager announced it curtly in front of others and wouldn’t answer questions. Which fairness type was violated?
questions.explanation: The outcome was fine (distributive OK). The manner of treatment and explanation was the problem, which is interactional. People who experience it tend to blame the boss personally.

questions.prompt: Staff are upset because raises were decided without any consultation, with no explanation of criteria and no way to appeal. Which fairness type is at issue?
questions.explanation: The complaint is about the process: no two-way communication, no appeals. That’s procedural fairness.

questions.prompt: Marco stays at his company only because leaving would cost him a generous pension and he sees no other job options. This is:
questions.explanation: Staying because of the costs of leaving ("have to") is continuance. It’s also the type that’s negatively related to performance.

questions.prompt: Which type of commitment is negatively related to job performance?
questions.explanation: Continuance commitment is negatively related to performance. Affective commitment boosts it.

questions.prompt: Canada and the US have similar Hofstede profiles on every dimension except:
questions.explanation: Both are low power distance, weak uncertainty avoidance, individualist and short-term. The US is more masculine than Canada.

questions.prompt: A culture that stresses rules, security and conformity, and treats hard work as a virtue, is high on:
questions.explanation: Discomfort with ambiguity and a preference for rules = strong uncertainty avoidance (e.g., Japan, Greece, Portugal).

questions.prompt: A call-centre agent must stay cheerful with rude callers and hide her irritation. This requirement is:
questions.explanation: Conforming to display rules regardless of true feelings is emotional labour. Suppressing negative emotion is the draining form.

questions.prompt: A server’s bad mood spreads to her table of customers. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Moods spreading between people = emotional contagion.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the textbook’s forms of OCB?
questions.explanation: This text lists helping, conscientiousness, being a good sport, and courtesy/cooperation. Civic virtue isn’t in it.

questions.prompt: In Salovey & Mayer’s four-branch model, the highest-level branch is:
questions.explanation: Perceive → Use → Understand → Manage (PUUM), lowest to highest.

questions.prompt: "Empathy, organizational awareness and service" make up which domain of Goleman’s competency model (lecture)?
questions.explanation: Those three are social awareness. Relationship management is influence, conflict management, teamwork and the rest.

questions.prompt: Which cultural-intelligence sub-skill appears in the lecture’s four-factor model but NOT in the textbook’s three components?
questions.explanation: The text lists knowledge, motivation and behaviour. The lecture adds Strategy (metacognitive).

questions.prompt: Research on ability and motivation supports which model of performance?

options.text: An additive model where each contributes independently
Ability matters only when motivation is high
Motivation matters only for low-ability workers

questions.explanation: The evidence supports an additive model, not the popular multiplicative one.

questions.prompt: Two employees report the same overall job satisfaction, but one loves the pay and hates the boss and the other the reverse. This illustrates:

options.text: The difference between facet and overall satisfaction

questions.explanation: Facet satisfactions can differ while the overall summary is the same.

questions.prompt: A friend quits a job she hated. Six months into the new job, her satisfaction has dropped again. This is the:
questions.explanation: Satisfaction rises after a job change (honeymoon), then falls as the new job’s flaws show (hangover).

questions.prompt: An MBTI "T" versus "F" describes:

options.text: How you make decisions: logic versus values and people
How you handle the outside world

questions.explanation: T/F is the deciding preference. E/I = energy, S/N = information, J/P = handling the world.

questions.prompt: Aiden misses a deadline every week. His teammates rarely miss deadlines, and he missed them regularly at his last co-op too. His manager will most likely attribute this to:
questions.explanation: High consistency (every week) + low consensus (teammates don’t) + low distinctiveness (the last job too) = dispositional. If workload were the cause, teammates would miss deadlines too.

questions.prompt: A manager calls a chronically late employee "irresponsible," ignoring that the bus route was cancelled. The employee blames the bus schedule. This pair of reactions illustrates:
questions.explanation: Actor = situational, observer = dispositional, for the same behaviour. That’s the actor–observer effect.

questions.prompt: A store manager rates nearly every employee "average," rarely using "excellent" or "poor" even though performance clearly varies. This is:
questions.explanation: Clustering ratings in the middle is central tendency. Leniency clusters at the high end.

questions.prompt: An interviewer sees two outstanding candidates, then rates an average third candidate "below average." This is most likely:
questions.explanation: The earlier candidates distorted the perception of the current one. That’s a contrast effect.

questions.prompt: Which statement about stereotypes is TRUE, according to the textbook?

options.text: Some stereotypes are accurate, and people hold favourable stereotypes of their in-groups
Stereotyping is most likely when the perceiver has extensive information

questions.explanation: The text says most, not all, are inaccurate. Favourable ones exist, and stereotyping thrives when the perceiver lacks information.

questions.prompt: A student takes full credit for an A ("I studied hard") but blames a C on "unfair questions." This is:
questions.explanation: Success → disposition, failure → situation, for one’s own outcomes. That’s self-serving bias.

questions.prompt: A new co-worker is labelled "high potential" because of his Stanford degree. Later, his declining performance is ignored. Which model best describes this?

options.text: Bruner’s model of the perceptual process

questions.explanation: Categorization, then cue selectivity, then categorization strengthened is Bruner’s model. This is the textbook’s own example.

questions.prompt: In the lecture’s five-stage perceptual process, "sensory overload" happens at which stage?
questions.explanation: Too many stimuli to process is a selection problem (stage 3). Remember "SOS, Oh I see."

questions.prompt: A manager expects a new hire to struggle, gives her fewer chances to shine, and she ends up performing poorly. This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Expectations led the person to behave consistently with them. That’s a self-fulfilling prophecy (on the lecture’s list).

questions.prompt: A dishonest employee assumes all his co-workers are padding their expense claims too. This is:
questions.explanation: Attributing your own thoughts and feelings to others is projection, and here it may also work as perceptual defence.

questions.prompt: An interviewer assumes a candidate who arrives very well-dressed must also be competent and reliable, with no evidence. Which error is on the lecture list but filed under rater errors in the textbook?
questions.explanation: One trait shaping the general impression is the halo effect.

questions.prompt: Women told a math test "shows gender differences" score lower than women who weren’t told. This is:
questions.explanation: Fear of confirming a stereotype lowers the target’s own performance. That’s stereotype threat.

questions.prompt: Employees believe management is competent, cares about their interests and sticks to sound principles. These are the three bases of:
questions.explanation: Ability + benevolence + integrity = trust ("ABI").

questions.prompt: Because the company supported her through a family crisis, Leila now volunteers for extra projects to "give back." This best reflects:

options.text: POS and the norm of reciprocity

questions.explanation: Strong perceived organizational support creates a felt obligation to reciprocate (organizational support theory).

questions.prompt: An applicant turns down an offer because the interviewer was dismissive and the tests felt unfair: "That’s probably what working there is like." This illustrates:
questions.explanation: Applicants read the selection experience as signals of what the organization is really like.

questions.prompt: Which pattern of cues produces a SITUATIONAL attribution in the textbook’s example (Mika)?

options.text: High consistency, high consensus, high distinctiveness
High consistency, low consensus, low distinctiveness
Low consistency, high consensus, low distinctiveness
Low consistency, low consensus, high distinctiveness

questions.explanation: Mika: High/High/High → situational. High/Low/Low is Roshani (dispositional). Low/High/Low is Sam (temporary situational).

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to reduce rater errors like halo and leniency?

options.text: Letting managers rate from memory at year end

questions.explanation: FOR training and behaviourally anchored rating scales are the textbook’s fixes.

questions.prompt: The tendency to overemphasize dispositional explanations for OTHER people’s behaviour is:
questions.explanation: That’s the definition of the fundamental attribution error.

questions.prompt: The perceiver’s tendency to screen out or distort information that would provoke unpleasant emotions is called:
questions.explanation: Perceptual defence is part of the perceiver component.

questions.prompt: In the expectancy diagram from the Week 4 lecture, a sales rep works hard and is skilled, but a supplier shortage leaves her with no stock to sell, so she misses her target. The diagram calls this kind of factor:
questions.explanation: Externalities are conditions outside the employee’s control (equipment, customer demand, supply) that affect performance and consequences.

questions.prompt: On slide 16’s expectancy diagram, “beliefs about outcome contingencies” are:
questions.explanation: Expectancies = beliefs about performance capabilities; instrumentalities = beliefs about outcome contingencies; valences = beliefs about outcome desirabilities.

questions.prompt: Priya just got a 6% raise, the biggest in her career, but she is angry because a colleague who does less got 8%. According to the Week 4 lecture, which strength of equity theory explains this?

options.text: Its emphasis on social comparison: relative perceptions matter more than the absolute reward
Its distinction between hygiene factors and motivators

questions.explanation: Equity theory explains why people can be demotivated even after a substantial reward: what matters is the comparison with others.

questions.prompt: According to the Week 4 lecture, autonomy in self-determination theory means:

options.text: Having choice and a sense of volition in what you do
Doing whatever you want without rules

questions.explanation: Autonomy = choice and volition. Dr. Kassaye stresses it does not mean doing whatever you want or working without rules (and the notes add: not independence).

questions.prompt: A student asks: “If I set a specific, challenging goal, is that enough?” Dr. Kassaye’s answer in the recorded lecture was:

options.text: No: you must commit to it, work toward it and use feedback to adjust
Yes: specific goals are sufficient on their own
Yes, as long as it is written as a SMART goal
No: goals only work when tied to money

questions.explanation: Setting a goal is only the start. Commitment, work and feedback make it effective.

questions.prompt: According to Herzberg’s two-factor theory (Week 4 lecture), which of these is a HYGIENE factor rather than a motivator?
questions.explanation: Salary is a hygiene factor: it prevents dissatisfaction but doesn’t create lasting motivation. Recognition, responsibility and advancement are motivators.

questions.prompt: A company fixes its outdated equipment and cramped offices and raises pay to market. Staff complaints drop, but effort doesn’t rise. Herzberg would say this is because:

options.text: Improving hygiene factors removes dissatisfaction but doesn’t motivate
Pay is a motivator but conditions are not
The firm skipped the esteem level of Maslow’s hierarchy

questions.explanation: Fixing hygiene factors gets people to “not dissatisfied.” To motivate, Herzberg says to add motivators: achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth, the work itself.

questions.prompt: In the Week 4 lecture, "content approaches" to motivation correspond to which textbook category?
questions.explanation: Content = need theories (Maslow, Herzberg, Alderfer, McClelland). “Cognitive/information-processing” = the textbook’s process theories.

questions.prompt: Which theory is NOT one of the lecture’s “cognitive / information-processing” approaches?
questions.explanation: Herzberg is a content (need) theory. Expectancy, equity and goal setting are the cognitive approaches.

questions.prompt: On slide 17’s expectancy table, an employee who is confident hard work will produce results and who values the reward, but who doubts performance will actually be rewarded, has what level of motivation?
questions.explanation: High expectancy, low instrumentality, high valence = Moderate. Any row with low expectancy is Low or Very low.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the O.B. Mod steps on the Week 4 slides?

options.text: Define target behaviour → set goals → measure frequency → monitor → administer rewards
Administer rewards → define behaviour → monitor → set goals → measure
Set goals → administer rewards → define behaviour → measure → monitor
Measure frequency → monitor → define behaviour → reward → set goals

questions.explanation: Define, Set, Measure, Monitor, Reward. Measure first establishes the baseline.

questions.prompt: A manager stops giving micromanaging check-ins to an employee once she consistently meets deadlines, and she keeps meeting them. According to the Week 4 lecture example, this is:
questions.explanation: Removing an unpleasant condition (close supervision) to strengthen a desired behaviour is negative reinforcement. This is the lecture’s own example.

questions.prompt: A sales manager says: "I don’t care how many calls you make. I care whether you close deals." Which property of motivation is she emphasizing?
questions.explanation: Channelling effort toward the outcomes that matter is direction ("working smart as well as hard").

questions.prompt: Denied a promotion she wanted for growth, Ana suddenly starts pushing hard for a bigger salary. Which theory best explains this?
questions.explanation: A frustrated higher need (growth) makes a lower need (existence) stronger. That’s frustration-regression, which is unique to ERG.

questions.prompt: According to McClelland, the most effective managers typically have:

options.text: High need for power and low need for affiliation
High need for affiliation and low need for power
Equal levels of all three needs

questions.explanation: High n Pow, low n Aff, with power directed at organizational goals. High affiliation is the intuitive trap.

questions.prompt: An employee believes that no matter how hard she works, she can’t hit the new quota. In expectancy terms, the problem is low:
questions.explanation: The effort → performance link is expectancy. With E ≈ 0, force ≈ 0 no matter the valence.

questions.prompt: Staff hit their targets, but past bonuses were often "forgotten" by management. Motivation is falling. Which component is damaged?
questions.explanation: The performance → outcome link is instrumentality. The fix is to make reward contingencies explicit and honour them.

questions.prompt: A worker learns a peer with the same job and effort earns more. Instead of complaining, she decides the peer "must have skills I don’t see." Which equity-restoring tactic is this?
questions.explanation: She perceptually inflates the other person’s inputs, which is distorting the comparison other.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of goal-setting theory’s four mechanisms?
questions.explanation: The four are attention, effort, persistence and strategies. Goal commitment is largely independent of money.

questions.prompt: Which goal orientation is NOT reliably related to learning or performance?

options.text: None: all three are strongly positive

questions.explanation: Learning orientation is positive, performance-avoid is negative, and performance-prove is the null result.

questions.prompt: SDT’s three universal needs are:
questions.explanation: SDT = CAR. ERG = existence/relatedness/growth. McClelland = achievement/affiliation/power.

questions.prompt: In the MPS formula, which change would drop a job’s score to near zero?

options.text: Autonomy falls to 1 out of 7 (near zero)

questions.explanation: Autonomy and feedback are multiplied. Variety, identity and significance are averaged, so they partly compensate for each other.

questions.prompt: A furniture plant turns four specialists (cutting, sanding, assembly, finishing) into "chair makers" who each build whole chairs. This mainly raises:
questions.explanation: Combining tasks raises variety and identity (a whole, identifiable piece of work).

questions.prompt: A cashier is given more register duties at the same skill level and calls it "enrichment." It is actually:
questions.explanation: Adding more same-level tasks (breadth only) is enlargement, which doesn’t raise the core characteristics.

questions.prompt: A plant pays a bonus when its own scrap and energy costs fall below a target formula, designed with heavy worker participation. This is:
questions.explanation: Bonuses for controllable unit-level gains are gainsharing (e.g., the Scanlon Plan). Profit sharing uses company-wide profits.

questions.prompt: Piece-rate workers informally agree never to produce more than 80 units a day, fearing management will "cut the rate." This problem is:
questions.explanation: An informal group output ceiling is restriction of productivity, a social problem on the wage-incentive list.

questions.prompt: A firm cuts everyone’s hours by 20% for six months instead of laying people off. This is:
questions.explanation: Reducing hours to avoid layoffs is work sharing. Job sharing is two people splitting one role.

questions.prompt: According to the research, MBO produces large productivity gains mainly when:

options.text: Top management is highly committed to it

questions.explanation: There was a 56% gain with high top-management commitment vs 6% with low.

questions.prompt: A manager stops nagging an employee once the employee files reports on time, and on-time filing increases. This is:
questions.explanation: Removing something unpleasant (nagging) to increase a behaviour = negative reinforcement.

questions.prompt: Every time an employee is late, the supervisor assigns the most unpleasant task, and lateness stops. This is:
questions.explanation: Adding an aversive stimulus to decrease behaviour = punishment.

questions.prompt: A trainee praised after every correct task learns fast, but her performance drops quickly once praise stops. Why?

options.text: Continuous, immediate reinforcement produces fast learning but low persistence
Extinction is impossible under continuous reinforcement

questions.explanation: Continuous reinforcement means fast in, fast out. Partial reinforcement produces more persistent behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a source of self-efficacy beliefs in social cognitive theory?
questions.explanation: The four sources are mastery, observation, verbal persuasion and physiological state.

questions.prompt: Flexible work arrangements are framed in the text as primarily intended to:

options.text: Meet diverse workforce needs and aid retention and satisfaction

questions.explanation: Unlike pay and job design, flex arrangements aren’t mainly about effort. They serve diverse needs, work–life balance and retention.

questions.prompt: Which merit-pay problem mainly damages employees’ equity perceptions?
questions.explanation: Without real information, employees invent salary estimates (overestimating peers’ pay), which damages equity. Low discrimination and small increases mainly hit instrumentality and valence.

questions.prompt: A supermarket manager wants to win back customers who have stopped coming but has no idea why they left. This is best described as:

options.text: An ill-structured problem calling for non-programmed decision making
A well-structured problem solved with a reorder rule
A programmed decision, because retail problems are repetitive
A well-structured problem, because the goal (more customers) is clear

questions.explanation: The desired state is clear but the existing state (why?) and the method are not, so it is ill-structured. Part of the job is defining the problem. The reorder example (120 units, 40 on hand, boxes of 10) is the well-structured one.

questions.prompt: In the Phoenix payroll case, the textbook treats “paying people their due salaries” and “putting into place the system to do it” as, respectively:
questions.explanation: A big project can contain both kinds. Classify the specific problem the question asks about.

questions.prompt: You have one week to find an apartment, so you set requirements for rent, commute and space, view listings until one meets all three, and sign. This is:

options.text: Satisficing, a response to bounded rationality
Maximizing, because you used explicit criteria

questions.explanation: Establishing an acceptable level and stopping at the first solution that exceeds it is satisficing. Maximizing would require inspecting every unit and computing the best expected value.

questions.prompt: The textbook’s rational decision-making model has ___ stages, while Dr. Kassaye’s “why bounded rationality occurs” list has ___ items.
questions.explanation: Exhibit 11.1 (and slide 6) = seven steps. Slides 9–18 give nine reasons for bounded rationality (framing, cognitive biases, problem identification, information search, alternatives, risk, implementation, solution evaluation, emotion and mood).

questions.prompt: A restaurant owner reasons: “This place looks like other successful restaurants, so its service must be excellent.” According to the Week 5A lecture, this is:
questions.explanation: Judging by resemblance to a familiar category is representativeness, a lecture-only term. Availability is about ease of recall (vivid, recent examples).

questions.prompt: A seller opens at $10,000 for a restaurant oven and “reduces” the price to $8,000. You feel you got a bargain, though comparable ovens sell for about $6,000. This is:
questions.explanation: The first number acted as an anchor, and the estimate of a fair price wasn’t adjusted enough. Defence: get independent price comparisons before negotiating.

questions.prompt: A hospital administrator sees rising nurse turnover and immediately announces a retention bonus without asking why nurses leave. Which problem-identification error is this?

options.text: Problem defined in terms of a solution (the plunging-in bias)
Problem defined in terms of functional specialty
Problem diagnosed in terms of symptoms

questions.explanation: The answer was chosen before the problem was diagnosed: Solution. (Symptom would be stopping at “we have a turnover problem.”)

questions.prompt: A company can settle a lawsuit for a sure loss of $25 million or go to court with a 50% chance of losing $50 million. Which is the most likely choice, and why?

options.text: Go to court: choices framed as losses encourage risk taking
Settle: the expected values are different
Indifference, because the expected values are equal

questions.explanation: Losses → Leap. The expected values are equal, but framed as a choice between losses about 80% pick the gamble. Reframed as gains, most pick the sure thing.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture’s slide on attitudes toward risk, a risk-averse decision maker:

options.text: Prefers a certain outcome to a gamble with the same expected monetary outcome
Prefers the gamble to the certain outcome
Will never gamble, even to avoid a sure loss

questions.explanation: Risk-averse = prefers certainty; risk-neutral = indifferent; risk-taking = prefers the gamble. A risk-averse person can still gamble when a sure loss is on the table. That is the framing effect, a separate idea.

questions.prompt: A manager says, “We’ve already spent $1 million, so we have to finish.” She is:

options.text: Escalating commitment because of sunk costs
Reasoning correctly, because sunk costs should drive the decision

questions.explanation: Sunk costs are the cause; escalation is the behaviour. Only future costs and benefits should drive the next decision.

questions.prompt: A newly appointed director inherits a failing project she did not start, yet keeps funding it because “taxpayers would think we squandered their money.” Which reason for escalation best fits?
questions.explanation: She didn’t make the original decision, so dissonance and consistency drop out. “Not appearing wasteful” (and framing) explain it, as with BC’s Site C dam.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a recommended way to prevent escalation of commitment?

options.text: Give the continue-or-stop decision to a group that includes the original project team
Set specific goals in advance that must be met before more resources are invested
Separate initial and subsequent decision making
Evaluate managers on how they made decisions more than on outcomes

questions.explanation: The text warns that groups are more prone than individuals to escalate. The other three are on the five-step prevention list.

questions.prompt: In the currency-trading simulation described in the text, which traders did best?
questions.explanation: Good-mood traders lost money; bad-mood traders did better but were conservative; neutral-mood traders did best, tolerating risk without overconfidence.

questions.prompt: According to Week 5B slide 4, the correct order of the basic model of communication is:

options.text: Thinking, encoding, transmitting, perceiving, decoding, understanding, feedback
Encoding, thinking, transmitting, decoding, perceiving, understanding, feedback
Thinking, transmitting, encoding, perceiving, understanding, decoding, feedback
Encoding, transmitting, decoding, understanding, feedback, thinking, perceiving

questions.explanation: Sender: Think, Encode, Transmit. Receiver: Perceive, Decode, Understand. Then Feedback back to the sender (“The Eager Teacher Prepares Daily Useful Feedback”).

questions.prompt: A salesperson’s idea must travel up through marketing and down through R&D to reach the R&D staff. This is ___ communication suffering mainly from ___.
questions.explanation: Between departments = horizontal; in a strict chain it goes up to a common manager and back down, which is slow. Direction (where) is not deficiency (why it fails).

questions.prompt: A junior developer finds a bug that will delay a launch but says nothing because she hopes for a promotion. Which concept best describes her behaviour?

options.text: Silence driven by the mum effect

questions.explanation: Withholding relevant information = silence; the specific tendency to avoid passing on unfavourable news is the mum effect (stronger when you want to impress). Filtering would be a message softened as it travels.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the conditions under which rumours spread fastest?

options.text: The information is clear and routine
The content is important to those involved

questions.explanation: Rumours spread fastest when the information is ambiguous, important, credible and the recipient is anxious (“Always Investigate Crazy Announcements”).

questions.prompt: The textbook lists two advantages of the grapevine. Which of these appears as a third “pro” only on the Week 5B slide?

options.text: Testing employee reactions to proposed changes

questions.explanation: The slide adds “a potential informal recruiting source.” The textbook’s two are keeping employees informed and testing reactions. The pipeline for rumours is the con.

questions.prompt: After a pitch, a manager tells a colleague, “You were great… one small thing on the pricing slide… otherwise fantastic,” and the colleague never fixes the slide. Which Tannen difference is most directly at work?

options.text: Feedback (buffering criticism with praise vs bluntness)

questions.explanation: Women tend to buffer criticism with praise; men tend to be blunt and may hear the praise as the main message. Per the lecture, treat these as tendencies, not fixed traits.

questions.prompt: A British executive calls a proposal “interesting” when she means “it’s rubbish.” Which cross-cultural dimension does the textbook use for this kind of example?
questions.explanation: Saying things you don’t literally mean to be polite is etiquette and politeness. Social conventions are directness, greetings, loudness, punctuality and personal information.

questions.prompt: Which statement is true of high-context cultures?

options.text: The message is strongly shaped by context, and lengthy contracts matter less than the relationship
People favour getting to the point quickly and very detailed contracts
North America and Scandinavia are typical examples

questions.explanation: High-context (many East Asian, Latin American, African, Arab cultures): meaning sits in the context, relationships come first and contracts matter less. The other options describe low-context cultures.

questions.prompt: The textbook’s second cross-cultural precaution is:
questions.explanation: Textbook: “recognize differences within cultures” (don’t stereotype). Slide 13 says “in cultures,” apparently dropping “within.” Use the textbook wording.

questions.prompt: A manager must tell an employee that her role is being eliminated. According to the information richness rule of thumb, the best medium is:

options.text: Face-to-face, which is highest in synchronization and cues
Email, to keep the message factual
A text message, because it is quick

questions.explanation: Less routine, emotional and important messages call for richer media. Email is lean: essentially one-way and without non-verbal or para-verbal cues.

questions.prompt: According to the research reviewed in the text, an inadequate explanation of a controversial decision is seen as:

options.text: Less fair than no explanation at all
About as fair as no explanation
Fairer than no explanation, because at least something was said

questions.explanation: An adequate explanation cut retaliation by 43%, but an inadequate explanation is seen as less fair than none.
